subjects.label: Jacobins under the Directory: repeated revival, containment and repression
subjects.meaning: Jacobin press, clubs and parliamentary activity revived in distinct Directorial cycles: post-Vendémiaire indulgence aided the Pantheon Club before closure; post-Fructidor constitutional circles rallied mixed anti-royalist republicans before democratic demands prompted restriction. In1799 press freedom, the Manège, appointments and emergency conscription, forced-loan and hostage measures renewed influence without a parliamentary majority. Official encouragement again gave way to hostile campaigning, eviction and Fouché’s closure of the Manège; rejection of Country in Danger contained emergency politics and served Sieyes’s constitutional-executive project. Jacobin efforts to impeach the former Directors and General Schérer rested on accusations of corruption; the indictments were ultimately rejected, not established as judicial findings.
subjects.stance: Pantheon, constitutional circles and Manège were distinct formations. Wartime emergency and anti-royalism created opportunities, but neither official encouragement nor electoral gains meant stable Jacobin control.

evidence.evidence_summary: Amnesty, press subsidies, renewed meetings, and the thousand-member Pantheon Club mark rapid Jacobin recovery.

Initial division over Babeuf gave way to sympathy after his wife’s arrest and applause for reunion with the Jacobins. The government then closed clubs and a theatre, purged suspects and criminalized advocacy of the1793constitution; sympathy is not proof of conspiracy membership.
Post-Fructidor clubs and constitutional circles formed across departments as intended republican rallying points, drawing many veterans of the revolutionary left.
Social and democratic demands and calls to widen suffrage led to closures; circles nevertheless helped defeat official candidates in the elections.
Press freedom, the Manège Club, official appointments, conscription, and a forced loan mark renewed Jacobin influence.

Hostage law and impeachment pressure alarmed Sieyès, whose executive project required containing the Jacobins. Schérer faced corruption accusations alongside the former Directors; after campaigning, eviction and Fouché’s closure of the Manège, the Five Hundred rejected the indictments.
Jourdan’s Country in Danger motion threatened renewed extraordinary powers and evoked fears of1793; its defeat before the later military successes marked the limit of Jacobin emergency influence.

source_treatments.stance: The two cycles illustrate tactical use without empowerment of the left. Neither Jacobins nor constitutional circles were a uniform organization; distinguish Babouvist conspiracy, broad republican mobilization, and later parliamentary ambitions.

subjects.label: Two Thirds Law
subjects.meaning: The Convention's requirement that two-thirds of the first Councils come from its own membership, together with ratification controversy and political backlash. subjects.stance: Presented as a continuity device born of constitutional anxiety but widely unpopular, electorally confused, and the immediate cause of the Vendémiaire confrontation.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Convention reserves two-thirds of the first Councils for its members, rejecting repetition of the1791self-denying break in legislative experience.

The constitution’s official vote of about 1.06 million to 49,000 may omit another 200,000 participants. The separate Two Thirds decree received barely 200,000 favourable votes out of 314,000 officially recorded amid confusion, widespread neglect and opposition. These are qualified reported returns, not a reliable common measure of popular assent; Parisian ballot-rigging accusations and sectional resistance follow.
Vendémiaire's defeat ensures the law operates and prolongs Thermidorian control until 1797.
